claims.text: Overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu coating at high temperature is governed by coating grain size and the resulting grain-boundary density.
Microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating during high-temperature sliding is governed by coating grain size and the resulting grain-boundary density.
The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has a grain size of 10 micrometers.
Controlled annealing can reduce the coating grain size from 10 micrometers to 1 micrometer.
The proposed predictions apply at 500-700 degrees Celsius, a sliding speed of 1 m/s, and a normal load of 10 N.
Reducing grain size from 10 micrometers to 1 micrometer increases grain-boundary density.
Grain boundaries act as obstacles to dislocation movement in the coating.
Increasing grain-boundary density enhances wear resistance by impeding dislocation movement.
Increasing grain-boundary density reduces microscopic deformation by impeding dislocation movement.
A 1-micrometer-grained coating will have better wear resistance than the 10-micrometer baseline coating under the stated conditions.
A 1-micrometer-grained coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation than the 10-micrometer baseline coating under the stated conditions.
Reducing grain size below 0.1 micrometers may decrease wear resistance.
The proposed loss of wear resistance below 0.1 micrometers is caused by increased susceptibility to grain-boundary sliding.
The grain-size–wear-resistance relationship may depend on substrate material and sliding conditions.
Failure of the 1-micrometer coating to show both improved wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation relative to the 10-micrometer coating would falsify the hypothesis.
